title: Acute lower GI bleeding
subtitle: Shock index first, localise before you operate

sources.title: Diagnosis and management of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding: guidelines from the British Society of Gastroenterology
Derivation and validation of a novel risk score for safe discharge after acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding (Oakland score)
Management of patients with acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding: an updated ACG guideline

red_flags.text: Shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) above 1: an unstable bleed by the BSG definition.
Haematochezia with shock: up to about one in seven of these bleeds is from an upper GI source.
Bleeding on anticoagulants or dual antiplatelet therapy, or after recent polypectomy.
Previous aortic surgery or an aortic graft with any GI bleed: think aorto-enteric fistula.
Ongoing transfusion requirement, or rebleeding after an apparent stop.

do_now.text: Calculate the shock index at the door. Above 1, resuscitate and treat as an unstable bleed.
Two large-bore cannulae, bloods including crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol for shock.
Restrictive red cell transfusion: threshold 70 g/L with a target of 70 to 90 g/L, or threshold 80 g/L and target 100 g/L with a history of cardiovascular disease.
Unstable patient: CT angiography first to localise the bleed, unless an upper GI source is suspected, in which case upper endoscopy comes first.

assess.text: Stable patients: calculate the Oakland score (age, sex, previous LGIB admission, rectal examination findings, heart rate, systolic pressure, haemoglobin). A score of 8 or less with no other reason to admit permits discharge with urgent outpatient investigation.
Drug history in detail: anticoagulant, antiplatelet, the indication for each, coronary stent dates, and recent dose changes.
Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy in every patient. Anorectal sources are common and easily missed.
Consider an upper source when the urea is raised disproportionately or the patient is shocked.

investigate.text: FBC, U&E, coagulation, group and crossmatch, venous gas with lactate.
CT angiography for the unstable patient, as the first localising test.
Colonoscopy on the next available list for stable patients who are admitted, after bowel preparation.
Upper GI endoscopy when no lower source is found or an upper source is suspected.
Small bowel evaluation (capsule or CT enterography) for a recurrent bleed with negative upper and lower endoscopy.

resuscitate.text: Warfarin: interrupt at presentation, and in unstable bleeding reverse with prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K.
Direct oral anticoagulants: interrupt; for life-threatening bleeding on dabigatran, consider idarucizumab. Reversal of factor Xa inhibitors follows local protocol and haematology advice.
Aspirin for primary prevention: stop permanently. Aspirin for secondary prevention: do not stop routinely, and if stopped, restart once haemostasis is achieved.

Dual antiplatelet therapy: continue aspirin; the P2Y12 inhibitor may be held only after discussion with cardiology, and not within 90 days of an acute coronary syndrome or 30 days of a coronary stent without that discussion.

definitive.text: Positive CT angiogram: catheter angiography and embolisation, ideally within 60 minutes in a centre with a 24/7 interventional radiology service.
Stable admitted patients: colonoscopy with endoscopic haemostasis for a stigmata-bearing lesion, such as a diverticular or post-polypectomy bleed.
Laparotomy only after every effort to localise the bleed radiologically or endoscopically, except in exceptional circumstances. Blind subtotal colectomy has high rebleeding and mortality.
Low-risk stable patients by Oakland score: discharge with urgent outpatient colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy.
Restart warfarin around 7 days after the bleed in most patients, sooner with bridging in high thrombotic risk, and decide DOAC restart with the prescriber.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon, interventional radiology and gastroenterology together for any unstable bleed.
Transfer to a centre with 24/7 interventional radiology when the local unit cannot provide it and the patient can be stabilised for transfer.
Cardiology before holding antiplatelets in a patient with a recent coronary stent.
Critical care for ongoing transfusion or organ dysfunction.

notes: Most lower GI bleeds stop spontaneously. The task is to identify the few that will not, and the shock index does that faster than anything else.
Localise before you operate. A surgeon who resects the wrong segment of colon has removed the colon and left the bleeding.
The rectal examination is the cheapest investigation and the one most often skipped.
